clue.text: Mad artists loose in theatre

definitions.note: the definition describes people whose work is in the theatre: playwrights

indicators.note: let loose, these letters run free and settle into a new order

explanation.surface: Crazed painters run riot inside a playhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loose' rearranges MAD ARTISTS; the definition is 'in theatre', meaning those whose work belongs to the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Playwrights are the writers whose work lives in the theatre.

clue.text: Antic of African Queen

definitions.meaning: an antic is a caper or prank, a sense of the old word for mischief
the legendary queen of Carthage in North Africa, of Virgil's Aeneid

explanation.surface: A prank played by a queen from Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at the film The African Queen; instead it is the Carthaginian queen of the Aeneid, and an old word for a prank.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a slang term for a caper and the name of Carthage's founding queen.

clue.text: "When April first / Unclos'd the — leaves" (John Clare, The Village Minstrel)

definitions.text: "When April first / Unclos'd the — leaves" (John Clare, The Village Minstrel)

parts.words: "When April first / Unclos'd the — leaves" (John Clare, The Village Minstrel)
parts.note: the missing word in Clare's line is a spring plant whose leaves unfurl in April, the lords-and-ladies

explanation.surface: A line from John Clare's poem with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: A literary gap-fill: the solver supplies the plant Clare names, the cuckoo-pint or lords-and-ladies, a British hedgerow plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Clare's quoted line names this woodland plant, whose leaves open in early spring.

clue.text: The laird of Ellangowan might become taller barman

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase could turn into something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: A tall barman could transform into a Scottish landowner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'might become' rearranges TALLER BARMAN. Ellangowan is the estate of the Bertram family in Walter Scott's novel Guy Mannering.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scott's Guy Mannering this Bertram is named as a laird, or landowner, of the Ellangowan estate.

clue.text: Passage from it inconclusive for Mrs Moore

definitions.text: Passage from it inconclusive for Mrs Moore

parts.words: Passage from it inconclusive for Mrs Moore
parts.note: in Forster's A Passage to ..., Mrs Moore sails home from the country but dies at sea, so her voyage away never ends

explanation.surface: A journey that a certain Mrs Moore never finished.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on Forster's title A Passage to India: Mrs Moore's passage the other way is cut short by her death on board.
explanation.definitionFit: The country Forster's Mrs Moore leaves, dying on the voyage, so her passage from it is never completed.

clue.text: Wordlist, dictionary, treasury, lexicon …

parts.note: the clue is itself a run of near-synonyms, just like an entry in a book of synonyms; the Greek root also means treasury

explanation.surface: A list of words for a list of words.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue acts out its answer: a string of related words, as in Roget, and the Greek source word means a treasure store.
explanation.definitionFit: A book of synonyms is a word list, and its Greek root means a storehouse or treasury.

clue.text: Genius of Wilkie Collins

parts.note: Wilkie Collins wrote a novel titled The ___ Genius, so the missing adjective completes it

explanation.surface: A remark on the brilliance of the Victorian novelist Wilkie Collins.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as praise of Collins's talent, but Genius is half a title: his 1886 novel The Evil Genius.
explanation.definitionFit: Completes the title of a Collins novel about a malign influence, a wicked spirit.

clue.text: Conductor knows they are on the fiddle and haven't paid for their seats

definitions.text: Conductor knows they are on the fiddle and haven't paid for their seats

parts.words: Conductor knows they are on the fiddle and haven't paid for their seats
parts.note: reads like a bus or train conductor spotting fare-dodgers, but the orchestral conductor knows his string players sit free and play the fiddle

explanation.surface: A ticket inspector catches cheating passengers who dodged their fares.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the fiddle' is British slang for cheating; here it is literal, as orchestral string players perform seated without buying tickets.
explanation.definitionFit: Orchestral string players play the fiddle and occupy seats on stage, which the music conductor oversees.

clue.text: Unfortunate dilemmas at harvest festival

indicators.note: these letters fall out badly and land jumbled in another order

explanation.surface: Awkward quandaries arise at the time of the harvest celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfortunate' rearranges DILEMMAS AT. Lammas, 1 August, is the old English festival of the first wheat harvest.
explanation.definitionFit: Lammas season was the English celebration of the first grain harvest, with loaves blessed in church.

clue.text: Sort of villain in melodrama (understudy said to have expired

parts.note: an understudy stands in for an actor, as a double does

indicators.note: said means we hear the words and spell a lookalike

parts.note: to have expired is to have died

explanation.surface: A stage villain whose stand-in is rumoured to be dead.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening bracket is never closed as printed. 'said' turns DIED into DYED; a deep-dyed or double-dyed villain is thoroughly wicked.
explanation.definitionFit: A thoroughly ingrained rogue, steeped twice in colour, like the wicked squire of Victorian melodrama.

clue.text: Blake's discreet nocturnal flyer

parts.note: in Blake's poem The Sick Rose an invisible creature flies in the night to destroy the flower

explanation.surface: A secretive night-flying creature from William Blake's poems.
explanation.walkthrough: Blake's lines run: 'The invisible worm / That flies in the night'. 'Discreet' stands for invisible.
explanation.definitionFit: Blake's invisible creature flying in the night is this crawling grub of The Sick Rose.

clue.text: Fine French month is a reversal for dramatist …

indicators.note: the two words is and a swap places, so the order they stand in the clue is reversed

parts.note: beau is French for fine or handsome
March is a month

explanation.surface: A French playwright's fortunes turn on a fine spring month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reversal' does not turn letters round: it swaps the order of the two clue words 'is a'. Beaumarchais wrote The Marriage of Figaro.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaumarchais wrote The Barber of Seville and The Marriage of Figaro, so he is a playwright.

clue.text: Novel heroine gets an inner (aka an unsuccessful shot)

indicators.note: a shot that misses goes astray, so these letters go wild and are rearranged

explanation.surface: An archer hits the ring just off the bullseye, a near miss.
explanation.walkthrough: In archery an inner is a shot just outside the bull. 'unsuccessful shot' rearranges AN INNER and AKA AN.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolstoy's tragic adulteress gives her name to his novel, so she is its leading lady.

clue.text: … and some horses (including the badly bred) for another

definitions.note: carries on from the previous clue, so it means another dramatist

indicators.note: including means one thing is held inside the other

parts.note: a string is a group of racehorses kept by one stable

indicators.note: badly means the letters are put wrongly, out of order

explanation.surface: A stable's horses include one with poor breeding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges 'bred' and 'including' puts the result inside the horses. The leading dots tie it to 11 Down, so 'another' means another dramatist.
explanation.definitionFit: August Strindberg, the Swedish author of Miss Julie, is a playwright like the one in 11 Down.

clue.text: Calvinistic doctrine reveals DNA sequence found with new American experts

parts.note: a gene is a stretch of DNA

indicators.note: new means the letters are made over in a fresh order

parts.note: mavins, or mavens, are experts in American slang

explanation.surface: Scientists announce a genetic discovery with help from US specialists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges MAVINS, the US Yiddish-derived word for experts, into VANISM. Geneva was Calvin's city.
explanation.definitionFit: Calvin taught in Geneva, so the Reformed teaching of his followers takes its name from that city.

clue.text: John Galt protagonist with a sense of belonging

definitions.text: John Galt protagonist with a sense of belonging

parts.words: John Galt protagonist with a sense of belonging
parts.note: Galt's novel of 1832 is narrated by a Scottish MP, and a person who belongs to a club is one of its insiders

explanation.surface: A character from a Scottish novel who feels he fits in.
explanation.walkthrough: John Galt was a Scottish novelist; his political satire is titled after its narrator, an MP for a pocket borough.
explanation.definitionFit: Galt's book is named for its parliamentarian narrator, and one who belongs to any body is part of it.

clue.text: One of those at Leonard Woolf's gate?

definitions.text: One of those at Leonard Woolf's gate?

parts.words: One of those at Leonard Woolf's gate?
parts.note: Leonard Woolf wrote a 1939 polemic titled after the uncivilised invaders said to stand at the gate

explanation.surface: A visitor waiting at the Woolfs' front gate.
explanation.walkthrough: Woolf's book Barbarians at the Gate warned of fascism; the clue makes one of its title figures a caller at his house.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Woolf's book names uncivilised invaders gathering at the gates of civilisation.

clue.text: Some petunia table decoration for part of Greek church

definitions.text: decoration for part of Greek church

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A petunia sits on the table as an ornament for a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes the run inside 'petunia table'. A Uniat church follows Greek rites but is in union with Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Uniat churches are Eastern-rite churches, many Greek Catholic, in communion with Rome.

clue.text: Composer with strange characters from tribe

indicators.note: the letters of the word are taken and made strange, put into another order

explanation.surface: A musician who writes with odd letters drawn from a clan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange characters from' rearranges TRIBE. Jacques Ibert was a French composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacques Ibert, French author of Escales, wrote music.

clue.text: What out-of-work actor did about art? (began again)

indicators.note: about means one piece goes round the other

parts.note: an actor between jobs is said to be resting

explanation.surface: An unemployed actor took up painting, then went back to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resting' is the theatrical euphemism for being out of work; 'about' puts the art inside it, and the bracket holds the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To start over is to begin a second time.

clue.text: Meredith's hunting-type county girl

parts.note: Diana was the Roman goddess of the hunt
Warwickshire is an English county, often shortened in its title

explanation.surface: A huntin', shootin' young lady from the shires in George Meredith's fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: George Meredith's heroine of Diana of the Crossways bears this name; Warwick is the county town giving the earldom its title.
explanation.definitionFit: The full name of the heroine of Meredith's Diana of the Crossways.

clue.text: "Miss Brass … opening the safe, brought from it a dreary — of cold potatoes, looking as eatable as Stonehenge" (The Old Curiosity Shop)

definitions.text: "Miss Brass … opening the safe, brought from it a dreary — of cold potatoes, looking as eatable as Stonehenge" (The Old Curiosity Shop)

parts.words: "Miss Brass … opening the safe, brought from it a dreary — of cold potatoes, looking as eatable as Stonehenge" (The Old Curiosity Shop)
parts.note: the gap in the Dickens sentence wants a word for a bleak expanse or barren stretch

explanation.surface: A passage from Dickens with one word removed.
explanation.walkthrough: A literary gap-fill from The Old Curiosity Shop: Sally Brass serves the starving maid a desolate expanse of leftover potatoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens likens the leftover potatoes to a dreary barren tract of land.

clue.text: Writer on love is frank

indicators.note: on means the writer comes alongside, placed after the love

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O
a pen is a writer

explanation.surface: An author who writes about love speaks candidly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts PEN after O.
explanation.definitionFit: Candid and frank both mean honest and not hiding anything.

clue.text: Venerable Eliot protagonist?

definitions.meaning: the Venerable is the title of the Anglo-Saxon monk and historian of Jarrow
George Eliot's novel Adam ___ is named for its hero, the carpenter

explanation.surface: Asking whether an aged figure is one of George Eliot's heroes.
explanation.walkthrough: The monk-historian is known as 'the Venerable'; George Eliot's first full novel is Adam Bede.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anglo-Saxon historian is styled the Venerable, and Eliot's carpenter hero shares the surname.

clue.text: Gradually cooked rice from Farrar

indicators.note: cooked means the letters are cooked up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Rice slowly simmered, from a recipe by someone named Farrar.
explanation.walkthrough: F W Farrar's Victorian school story is titled with its hero's name, subtitled Little by Little, hence 'Gradually'. 'cooked' rearranges RICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Farrar's school novel is named for its schoolboy hero and subtitled Little by Little.

clue.text: Review arms simple investigator

indicators.note: to review is to look over again, so these letters are revised into a new order

explanation.surface: A critic sizes up an uncomplicated weapons expert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Review' rearranges ARMS SIMPLE. Agatha Christie's elderly sleuth of St Mary Mead.
explanation.definitionFit: Christie's spinster sleuth solves crimes, so she is a detective.

clue.text: London pastime

definitions.meaning: Jack London wrote a boxing novella titled The ___
a pastime is a sport or amusement

explanation.surface: A diversion enjoyed in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: London is not the city but Jack London, the American author of the boxing story The Game.
explanation.definitionFit: A sport or amusement, and the title of a Jack London prize-fight novella.

clue.text: Hidden meaning of Austen work found here in index

parts.note: in an index an entry is listed beneath its heading, so where to find it is beneath its key word
Sense and Sensibility is a Jane Austen novel, here shortened to its first word

explanation.surface: Looking up a Jane Austen novel in a book's index for its subtext.
explanation.walkthrough: In an index Austen's novel would be filed beneath its first word, so 'found here in index' gives the word for beneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A subtext or undercurrent of meaning lies below the surface sense of words.
